summary: Gives a mission statement for the IETF, defines the terms in it, argues why such a statement is needed, and records some of the debate that led to it.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3935 is the IETF's own answer to a simple question: what is the IETF for? It says the goal is to make the Internet work better, and it lists five principles the community works by. It also defines the words it uses, so that people outside the IETF can argue about its work in the same terms.

questions: what is the ietf mission statement
what are the ietf cardinal principles
what does rough consensus and running code mean
subtitle: The IETF states what it is for, defines the words it uses, and lists the five principles its work follows.

tldr.problem: The IETF has to make choices about what to work on, and people acting on its behalf sometimes decide without consulting the whole community. Without a shared statement of purpose, those choices are hard to judge.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC states the mission, defines the terms it uses, and sets out five cardinal principles: open process, technical competence, a volunteer core, rough consensus and running code, and protocol ownership.
tldr.outcome: The mission gives the IETF a test for any proposal: does this help or hinder making the Internet work better? The document is a Best Current Practice, BCP 95.

today: RFC 3935 is a Best Current Practice document, BCP 95, published in October 2004. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Mission and Its Five Principles
sections.content:
The goal of the IETF is to make the Internet work better. Its mission is to produce high quality, relevant technical and engineering documents that influence the way people design, use and manage the Internet in such a way as to make the Internet work better. Those documents include protocol standards, best current practices and informational documents of various kinds.

The mission is pursued by adhering to five cardinal principles. Open process means any interested person can take part in the work, know what is being decided and make his or her voice heard, and it commits the IETF to making its documents, working group mailing lists, attendance lists and meeting minutes publicly available on the Internet. Technical competence means the issues the IETF writes about are ones where it has the competence to speak, that it is willing to listen to technically competent input from any source, and that its output is expected to sound network engineering principles. Volunteer core means participants and leaders come because they want to do work that furthers the mission. Rough consensus and running code means standards rest on the combined engineering judgement of the participants and on real-world experience implementing and deploying the specifications. Protocol ownership means the IETF accepts responsibility for all aspects of a protocol it owns, even aspects that rarely or never appear on the Internet, and does not try to control protocols it does not own, even when they touch or affect the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF says its job is to make the Internet work better, and it does that by writing standards, best current practices and informational documents. Five principles guide the work: open process, technical competence, a volunteer core, rough consensus and running code, and protocol ownership.

sections.title: The Words the Statement Uses
sections.content:
The RFC defines the terms it depends on. A mission is what an organization sets out to do, in contrast to its goal, which is what it hopes to achieve, and its activities, which are the specific actions it takes. The Internet is a large, heterogeneous collection of interconnected systems that can be used for communication of many different types between any interested parties connected to it. The term covers both the core Internet, meaning ISP networks, and the edge Internet, meaning corporate and private networks often reached through firewalls, NAT boxes and application layer gateways.

A standard, as used here, is a specification of a protocol, system behaviour or procedure that has a unique identifier and where the IETF has agreed that if you want to do this thing, this is the description of how to do it. It does not mandate use and the IETF does not police it. Its benefit is interoperability: several products that implement a standard can work together. Participants are the individuals who take part in the process, and the RFC says the process works best when focused around people rather than around organizations, companies, governments or interest groups. Quality means expressing ideas clearly enough that everyone building systems to them understands them the same way, and describing the properties of a system well enough to understand its important consequences and ensure they benefit the Internet as a whole. Relevant means useful to some group of people who have to make decisions that affect the Internet; it does not mean correct or positive, so a report of a failed experiment or a specification that says why not to use something can be highly relevant.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC defines the words it uses so that people can argue about the IETF's work in the same terms. A standard here is a description of how to do something, not a rule that forces anyone to do it, and its value is that different products built from it can work together.

sections.title: Why a Mission Statement Is Needed
sections.content:
The IETF has to make decisions, and in some cases people acting on its behalf have to make decisions without consulting the entire IETF first. There are many reasons for this, including the near-impossibility of getting an informed consensus opinion on a complex subject out of a community of several thousand people in a short time.

Having a defined mission is one of the steps available for evaluating alternatives. Does a proposal help or hinder the mission, or is it orthogonal to it? If resources are limited, are there things they could be invested in that help the mission better? The RFC adds another step, which is to choose leaders trusted to exercise good judgement and do the right thing, but notes that the IETF is already trying to do that.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF often has to decide without asking everyone first, because a community of thousands cannot agree quickly on complex questions. A written mission gives people a test for proposals: does this help make the Internet work better, or not?

sections.title: Drawing the Boundary of the Work
sections.content:
A very difficult issue in discussing the mission is how wide the phrase "for the Internet" reaches, because the Internet is used for many things the IETF has neither interest nor competence in making standards for. The RFC proposes that the fairest balance is struck by this formulation: protocols and practices for which secure and scalable implementations are expected to have wide deployment and interoperation on the Internet, or to form part of the infrastructure of the Internet. The principle of competence adds a second limit: where the IETF does not have, and cannot gather, the competence needed to make technically sound standards, it should not attempt to take the leadership.

The RFC also separates the mission from the methods used to reach it. The appeals procedure is defined so that violations of the fundamental principles of technical competence and open process can be detected; it is not itself a fundamental value. Likewise, the question of which body declares a document ready for publication is entirely outside the mission statement, and the RFC says it is easy to imagine changing that without affecting the mission at all, even though it would change how well the mission could be achieved. The Internet is a global phenomenon, so the IETF keeps the emphasis on technical competence, rough consensus and individual participation, stays open to competent input from any source, and uses English for its work because of its utility in a global context. On protocol ownership, the IETF sometimes defines standards that end up used mostly outside the global Internet, and continues to administer them; it also leverages standards defined and maintained by other organizations and works with those organizations instead of taking them over.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC limits the IETF's work to protocols and practices meant to be deployed widely and to work with other implementations, or that become part of the Internet's infrastructure. It also separates the goal from the process: the appeals procedure and the publication rules are tools, not values.

sections.title: Research, Invention and Adoption
sections.content:
The IETF has traditionally been a community for experimentation with things that are not fully understood, for standardization of protocols for which some understanding has been reached, and for publication of, and refinement of, protocols originally specified outside the IETF process. All of these activities produce documents, but the documents should be judged by very different criteria when the time to publish comes around, and it is not uncommon to see people confused about what documents are in which category.

When deciding whether these activities should be done inside the IETF, the RFC says one should not chiefly look at the type of activity but at the potential benefit to the Internet. An experiment that yields information showing an approach is not viable might benefit the Internet more than publishing a standard that is technically competent but useful only in a few special cases. For research of an essentially unbounded nature, with an unknown probability of success, it may be more relevant to charter a research group than a standards group. For activities with a bounded scope, such as specifying several alternative protocols to the point where experiments can identify the better one for standardization, the working group mechanism may be the appropriate tool.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF does three kinds of work: experiments, standards, and adopting work done elsewhere. The RFC says to judge each by how much it helps the Internet, not by what kind of activity it is.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says that considering security is one of the core principles of sound network engineering for the Internet. Apart from that, security is not relevant to the memo itself. The document sets out how the IETF decides what to work on and how it argues about its own process; it defines no protocol, no message format and no mechanism that could be attacked.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo has little to say about security, because it defines no protocol. It notes only that thinking about security is one of the core principles of good network engineering.

items.title: Open process
items.text: Anyone can take part, know what is being decided and be heard. Documents, mailing lists and minutes are public.

items.title: Technical competence
items.text: The IETF speaks only where it has the competence, listens to competent input from any source, and expects sound engineering.

items.title: Volunteer core
items.text: Participants and leaders come because they want to do work that furthers the mission.

items.title: Rough consensus and running code
items.text: Standards rest on the participants' engineering judgement and on real experience implementing them.

items.title: Protocol ownership
items.text: The IETF takes responsibility for what it owns and leaves alone what it does not.
